summary.text: Plants are eukaryotic organisms of the kingdom Plantae, mostly living on energy from sunlight and mostly made of many cells.
About 380,000 species are known, and roughly 85 to 90 percent of all plant species are flowering plants.
They range from single cells to the tallest trees, and the sugars they make from sunlight power most of Earth's ecosystems.

items.prompt: A greenhouse worker wonders how a tray of seedlings feeds itself when nothing edible is added to the soil. What explains it for most plants?

options.label: Their roots absorb ready-made sugars from the soil and then burn them for energy
Green pigment in their chloroplasts captures sunlight to build sugars from carbon dioxide and water
Their leaves take in oxygen and turn it into stored food for the whole plant
Their cells release digestive enzymes that break down dead matter around them

items.explain: Most plants are photosynthetic: chlorophyll in chloroplasts lets them make sugars from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight.

items.prompt: An old biology book lists mushrooms and seaweed alongside oaks as one living group. What does today's definition say about mushrooms?

options.label: They stay in, because they grow fixed in the ground like oaks
They stay in, because they gather energy from sunlight like leaves
They stay in only when they grow on living trees
They are left out, because current definitions exclude fungi

items.explain: Historically the plant kingdom held everything that was not an animal, including algae and fungi. Definitions have narrowed since, and current ones exclude fungi and some algae.

items.prompt: If you picked one plant species at random from all those accepted, which kind would you most likely get?

options.label: A flowering plant
A moss
A fern
A conifer

items.explain: About 85 to 90 percent of all plant species are flowering plants, so a random pick almost surely lands there.

items.prompt: A wilted lettuce leaf is soaked and its cells fill up. What lets a plant cell take on that much liquid without bursting?

options.label: Its chloroplasts, which soak up the extra liquid as it arrives
A thick cell membrane that stretches without limit
A strong, flexible wall made mostly of cellulose, outside the cell membrane
A second nucleus that pumps the extra liquid back out

items.explain: Plant cells have a strong flexible cell wall outside the membrane, made mostly of cellulose, so they can swell with water without bursting.

items.prompt: A farmer clears every green plant from a valley. Why will nearly everything else living there struggle?

options.label: Animals can only breathe air that plants have filtered of dust
Sugars from plant photosynthesis supply the energy most ecosystems run on
Plants supply the minerals that animals normally get from rock
Without green cover, animals have no shade and overheat

items.explain: The sugars plants make by photosynthesis provide the energy for most of Earth's ecosystems, and other organisms depend on plant materials.

items.prompt: A biologist uses the broad sense of the word and counts both a drifting desmid and a towering Eucalyptus regnans. Is that a mistake?

options.label: Yes, anything counted must have roots, stems and leaves
Yes, only trees count under any definition
Yes, single-celled organisms belong to the fungus kingdom
No, in the broad sense plants run from single cells up to the tallest trees

items.explain: Plants in a broad sense range from single-celled desmids to the largest trees such as Eucalyptus regnans.

paragraphs.heading: What counts as a plant
paragraphs.text: Plants are the eukaryotic organisms that make up the kingdom Plantae. Most of them live on sunlight, or descend from ancestors that did: they use the green pigment chlorophyll in their chloroplasts to turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars. Over time some plants became parasites, taking their energy from other organisms instead. Most plants are built from many cells; the exceptions are glaucophytes, a few red algae and some green algae.

paragraphs.heading: A kingdom that shrank
paragraphs.text: In Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom held every living thing that was not an animal, algae and fungi included. Aristotle sorted beings by whether they had a "sensitive soul"; plants, in his scheme, had only a "vegetative" one. His student Theophrastus carried on classifying plants. Much later Carl Linnaeus laid the base of modern scientific classification but kept the plant kingdom, naming it Vegetabilia. Today's definitions are narrower and leave out fungi and some algae.

paragraphs.heading: The green plants today
paragraphs.text: One modern definition equates plants with the green plants, Viridiplantae. That group holds the green algae plus the land plants: flowering plants, conifers and other gymnosperms, ferns, lycophytes, mosses, liverworts and hornworts. About 382,000 species are accepted, and some 283,000 of them make seeds. Flowering plants alone are about 85–90% of all plant species. They range from single-celled desmids about 10 micrometres across to the conifer Sequoia sempervirens, which can stand 120 metres tall.

paragraphs.heading: From water onto land
paragraphs.text: The ancestors of land plants evolved in water. A scum of algae formed on land 1,200 million years ago, but the first land plants, organised like bryophytes, only appeared in the Ordovician, about 450 million years ago. Early land plants started to diversify around 420 million years ago in the late Silurian, and bryophytes, club mosses and ferns then turn up as fossils. By the end of the Devonian, plants had most of their modern basic features, including roots, leaves and, in trees like Archaeopteris, secondary wood.

paragraphs.heading: Forests, seeds and flowers
paragraphs.text: In the Carboniferous, forests grew in swamps, dominated by clubmosses and horsetails, some as large as trees. Early gymnosperms, the first seed plants, appeared then too. The Permo-Triassic extinction reshaped communities, which may have opened the way for flowering plants to evolve in the Triassic, about 200 million years ago. Charles Darwin called their rapid spread in the Cretaceous "an abominable mystery". Conifers diversified from the Late Triassic and came to dominate floras in the Jurassic.

paragraphs.heading: Why plants matter
paragraphs.text: Green plants supply a large share of the world's oxygen. The sugars they make by photosynthesis power most of Earth's ecosystems, and animals either eat plants or rely on plant materials in other ways. Grain, fruit and vegetables are staple human foods that people have domesticated over thousands of years. We also use plants for wood to build with, for ornaments and writing materials, and for a great many medicines. The scientific study of plants is called botany.
